issues.description: In Experiment 1, 17 out of 40 participants (42.5%) were excluded from analysis due to too few high confidence critical trials. In Experiment 2, 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded. These very high exclusion rates raise serious concerns about the generalizability of the findings, as the analyzed sample may be systematically different from the broader population. Participants who give fewer high-confidence responses may be those who are less susceptible to the illusion, meaning the exclusion procedure could artificially inflate the observed effect.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The entire analysis strategy conditions on high-confidence trials only, but the proportion of high-confidence trials varies dramatically across participants (e.g., range 3.6–93.2% in Experiment 1). By analyzing only high-confidence trials, the authors are selecting a non-random subset of trials that may systematically differ in ways that inflate the illusion effect. Participants who are more confident overall contribute more data, and the relationship between confidence and accuracy may itself be modulated by the experimental conditions. This creates a form of collider bias.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 53.8% high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: 36.3 – 93.2, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the text states that exclusion of participants with 10 or fewer high confidence critical trials resulted in inclusion of 23 participants with 5 excluded. But 40 - 5 = 35, not 23. The numbers do not add up, suggesting either a reporting error or an additional undisclosed exclusion criterion. This is a serious transparency issue.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: Confound between delay and interference conditions
issues.description: In Experiments 1 and 2, the 'Long' delay condition differs from the 'Short' condition in both the time elapsed AND the temporal proximity to the irrelevant second display. In Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appears 5 seconds after memory display offset in all conditions, meaning the interval between the cue and the second display differs across conditions. This creates confounds that make it difficult to attribute differences purely to memory decay versus interference or other temporal factors.
issues.quote: If the probe was presented 3 seconds after offset of the memory display (the Long condition), it appeared in isolation. If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display did not always contain both the target and its mirrored counterpart. For pseudo-letter targets, the real counterpart appeared on only half of critical trials, and for real-letter targets, the pseudo counterpart appeared on only 16% of trials. This asymmetry in response options creates different base rates for the opportunity to make illusory errors across conditions, complicating interpretation. While the authors acknowledge this and address it in Experiment 2, the Experiment 1 results are still presented as supporting evidence.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly define how error rates are calculated. It is unclear whether the error rates represent the proportion of all high-confidence trials that are errors, or the proportion of all trials (including low-confidence) that are high-confidence errors, or some other metric. The denominator matters substantially for interpretation, especially given the variable rates of high-confidence responding across participants and conditions.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Unequal base rates for error types
issues.description: The comparison between 'illusory errors' (selecting the mirrored counterpart) and 'other errors' (selecting any unrelated distractor) is not a fair comparison because there is only one mirrored counterpart but multiple unrelated distractors. If the 'other error' rate represents the probability of selecting any single other distractor, this should be stated explicitly. If it represents the total probability of selecting any distractor, then the comparison is between a single specific error and a pooled category, which have different chance levels.
issues.quote: Expectation-induced errors occurred more often than other errors (BFincl > 1000 for Error Type)

issues.subcategory: Response bias not adequately ruled out
issues.description: The authors dismiss response bias as an explanation with minimal justification. Participants may simply prefer selecting familiar stimuli (real letters) over unfamiliar ones (pseudo-letters) when uncertain, even on trials they rate as high confidence. The confidence rating itself may be inflated when selecting a familiar category. The authors state 'the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias' but do not provide a formal test or model to distinguish these accounts.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: Confidence ratings conflated with memory accuracy
issues.description: The authors assume that high confidence responses reflect genuine memory traces rather than guesses. However, confidence can be inflated by familiarity with the response category (real letters are more familiar). A participant who is uncertain but selects a real letter may feel more confident in that selection precisely because real letters feel more familiar, not because they have a genuine memory trace. This metacognitive bias would produce exactly the pattern observed: high-confidence pseudo-to-real errors.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.subcategory: Online data collection without adequate control
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom with participants using their own laptops. This introduces substantial variability in display conditions (screen size, resolution, refresh rate, viewing distance, ambient lighting) that could affect the perception and encoding of briefly presented stimuli (250 ms). The lack of standardized viewing conditions is particularly problematic for a study about visual memory of letter orientations.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: Optional stopping with sequential Bayes Factor
issues.description: In Experiments 3 and 4, the authors used a sequential Bayes Factor stopping rule, checking every other day of testing. While sequential testing with Bayes Factors is more robust than with p-values, the specific implementation details matter. The stopping thresholds differed between experiments (BF=6 in Experiment 3, BF=10 in Experiment 4) without justification, and the stopping rule was applied to a specific comparison (the critical t-test) rather than the full model, which could lead to underpowered tests for other effects of interest.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: Experiment 1 uses a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2-4 use a 4-point scale (1=guess, 4=certainty). The manuscript does not explain how 'high confidence' is defined on the 4-point scale (is it ratings of 3-4? Only 4?). This inconsistency makes it difficult to compare results across experiments and raises questions about whether the same construct is being measured.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: In the Results section of Experiment 4, the text refers to 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but Figure 5 was already used for Experiment 3. Based on the figure caption later in the text, this should be 'Figure 6'.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: Table 4 (follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory errors in Experiment 2) shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay and BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type. However, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets.' The BFincl values in the text do not match the table. The table shows strong evidence for Target Type but evidence against Memory Delay, which contradicts the text.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.description: In Table 4, the BFincl values for Memory Delay (0.064) and Target Type (39110.895) appear to be swapped relative to what the text describes. The text says Memory Delay had BFincl=190 and that target type did not matter for non-illusory errors, but the table shows the opposite pattern. Either the table labels are swapped or there is a serious error in the reported statistics.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42

issues.description: The authors argue that the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors rules out visual similarity as an explanation. However, this asymmetry could also be explained by differential discriminability: real letters may have sharper, more distinctive memory representations due to extensive prior exposure, making them easier to discriminate from their mirror counterparts. This is a memory strength account, not a 'world knowledge reshaping memory' account, and the authors do not adequately distinguish between these alternatives.
issues.quote: Another cause of illusory reports could be confusion between the to-be-remembered target and the mirrored counterpart that is presented in the response screen. However, Experiment 1 shows that pseudo-to-real illusions were much more prevalent than real-to-pseudo illusions.

issues.subcategory: Training and exclusion procedure only in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 included a training phase with a 75% accuracy threshold to ensure participant motivation and proficiency. Experiments 2-4 did not include this training, relying instead on brief practice trials. This inconsistency means that participant quality may differ across experiments, and the lack of training in later experiments (especially the large Experiment 2 with 290 participants from a course requirement) may introduce more noise or unmotivated participants.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.description: The increase in illusory errors over time is interpreted as evidence that illusions arise in memory rather than perception. However, this logic assumes that perceptual encoding is complete and identical across delay conditions. If participants engage in different post-perceptual processing strategies depending on the expected delay (e.g., verbal recoding), or if the cue timing affects retroactive interference differently, the delay manipulation does not cleanly separate perception from memory.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.description: The authors conduct multiple Bayesian ANOVAs and follow-up tests across four experiments without any correction or acknowledgment of the multiplicity of tests. While Bayesian methods are somewhat more robust to this issue than frequentist methods, the selective reporting of follow-up tests (e.g., reporting BFs for specific t-tests only when they support hypotheses) could still lead to biased conclusions.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type showed that for illusory errors, the optimal model consisted of the factors Memory delay, Target type and the interaction between the two

issues.description: The Experiment 1 methods state that 40 participants remained after training exclusions, but then only 23 were included in the analysis (with '5 participants excluded'). This leaves 12 participants unaccounted for. The discrepancy is not explained.
issues.quote: The remaining 40 participants... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Participants were 'explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters' and received trial-by-trial feedback. This instruction, combined with feedback showing errors, could create demand characteristics where participants become hyper-aware of the real/pseudo distinction and adopt strategies (like defaulting to real letters when uncertain) that could be mistaken for memory illusions.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.description: The study uses only mirrored letters as pseudo-letters. The conclusions about 'world knowledge shaping STM' are drawn from this single stimulus category. It is unclear whether these findings would generalize to other types of stimuli where expectations might differ (e.g., rotated objects, color changes, spatial configurations). The authors acknowledge this limitation only briefly when discussing Chalk et al.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report the priors used in the Bayesian ANOVAs conducted in JASP. The default priors in JASP may not be appropriate for all effect sizes expected in this paradigm, and the choice of priors can substantially influence Bayes Factors, especially for moderate effects.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayes Factors but does not report standardized effect sizes (e.g., partial eta-squared, Cohen's d) for any of the effects. Effect sizes are important for evaluating the practical significance of the findings and for future meta-analyses and power calculations.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18

issues.description: The authors argue that Fuzzy Trace Theory cannot explain their findings because FTT predicts that high similarity should facilitate false memories, and their stimuli are highly similar yet produce abundant false memories. This argument is contradictory - the authors seem to be saying FTT is wrong because it predicts what they found. The actual issue they raise (asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo) is a more valid criticism but is not clearly articulated.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: Feedback may alter strategy across experiment
issues.description: Trial-by-trial and block-by-block feedback was provided in all experiments. This feedback could lead participants to change their response strategies over the course of the experiment. For instance, after receiving feedback that they incorrectly reported a real letter when a pseudo-letter was shown, participants might become more cautious, potentially reducing the illusion effect over blocks. Alternatively, feedback about errors might increase anxiety and reduce confidence ratings. No analysis of learning effects or block-by-block trends is reported.
issues.quote: After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance. The main experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 20 trials. After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy.

issues.description: In the training section, rectangles are described as 0.05° × 0.01° in size, which would be essentially invisible (less than 1 arcminute). This is likely a reporting error - the actual stimuli were probably much larger.
issues.quote: eight white rectangles (0.05◦ × 0.01◦ in size)

issues.description: The manuscript consistently uses 'she' and 'her' to refer to participants, despite having mixed-gender samples. While minor, this is inconsistent with current reporting standards that recommend gender-neutral language.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment

issues.description: None of the four experiments appear to have been preregistered. Given the multiple experiments with different designs, exclusion criteria, and analysis strategies, preregistration would have been valuable for establishing that the hypotheses and analysis plans were determined a priori rather than adapted based on results.

The authors claim their findings show illusions in working memory and fragile memory stages of STM, but acknowledge they did not test iconic memory. Despite this, they make broad claims about 'all stages of STM' being susceptible to illusions, which is not supported by their data.
issues.quote: Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM, which is sometimes thought not to be susceptible to illusions based on contextual information or internally generated biases.

issues.description: The authors use non-standard Bayes Factor interpretation thresholds. They describe BF > 10 as 'strong evidence' and BF 3-10 as 'substantial evidence,' whereas the conventional Jeffreys scale considers BF 3-10 as 'moderate' or 'substantial' and BF 10-30 as 'strong.' More importantly, they treat BF < 0.33 as 'strong evidence for the null' when this is conventionally considered only 'moderate' evidence. This could lead to overstatement of evidence strength.
issues.quote: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 3 – 10: substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, >10: strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis
